title: Firms the City pays that settled or admitted federal fraud matters
question: Which firms on the City ledger have settled, admitted or been sued over federal fraud or false-claims matters, and what has the City paid them?
finding: 10 firms or groups on the City ledger appear in 16 Justice Department announcements since 2015. Local matters include the teacher residency program in San Francisco schools and two other federal cases. Tetra Tech EC agreed in 2026 to pay $57.0 million over soil tests at the Hunters Point shipyard (allegations only; the City has paid Tetra Tech companies $582,047 since fiscal 2019), and three San Francisco refuse companies admitted bribery and paid $36.0 million in 2021 (the City has paid Recology companies $114.4 million). The rest concern federal business elsewhere; the largest City payee among them is Kaiser Permanente affiliates ($3.92 billion, 100% of it paid by the Health Service System). Separately, the airport repaid the Federal Aviation Administration $809,554 in 2015 for costs wrongly billed to federal grants.
how: A fixed list of 16 firm names was checked against the titles of the 124 Justice Department civil-settlement releases that name a Bay Area place, and against the City ledger for fiscal years 2019 to 2026 (firms paid under $100,000 are left out unless the matter concerns work in San Francisco). The stage follows the issuing record. The Hunters Point and teacher residency entries also use a later federal recovery announcement and the signed settlement, respectively. The same release issued by two offices is counted once. The Hunters Point file on disk holds 88 documents: court orders, EPA and Navy reviews, and the settlement papers.
limits: A settlement is not an admission unless the release says so, and each row gives the stage the release itself states. Most of these matters concern Medicare, federal contracts or consumer law and have nothing to do with City work; a parent company's settlement does not mean the unit the City pays did anything wrong. The Hunters Point clean-up was paid for by the Navy, not the City. City payments are matched by vendor name, include affiliates, and for the health plans are mostly employee insurance premiums.
